After a short break from Angular, I’m rebuilding my skills by developing an Employee Management Portal using the latest version of Angular. My goal isn’t just to complete another CRUD application, but to understand the reasoning behind modern Angular practices and enterprise application architecture.
Today was focused on creating the Login page, but it turned out to be much more than designing a simple form.
What I Built
Today’s implementation included:

• Login page using Angular Material

• Reactive Forms

• Email and Password validation

• Show/Hide Password functionality

• Remember Me checkbox

• Forgot Password link (UI)

• Loading state for the Sign In button

• Responsive login card for different screen sizes
Although these features seem straightforward, every implementation raised an opportunity to learn something new.

Key Angular Concepts I Learned
One of the biggest takeaways was learning the modern Dependency Injection approach using inject() instead of constructor injection.
private readonly fb = inject(FormBuilder);This also introduced me to the TypeScript readonly modifier and why it's a good practice for injected dependencies.
Another interesting concept was using Typed Reactive Forms with nonNullable.group(). It improves type safety and removes unnecessary null checks, making the code cleaner and easier to maintain.
I also replaced the traditional *ngIf with Angular's new @if control flow syntax. Since *ngIf is now deprecated in newer Angular versions, it was a good opportunity to start following the latest recommendations.

Angular Material Learnings
Working with Angular Material taught me that even UI components involve architectural decisions.
Some topics I explored today were:

• Choosing appearance="outline" instead of fill for enterprise applications

• Understanding different Material button styles (mat-button, mat-flat-button, mat-stroked-button, mat-icon-button)

• Using matSuffix for the password visibility toggle

• Displaying validation messages using mat-error

• Adding a loading spinner during login
One interesting challenge was styling the Material spinner. I learned how Angular’s View Encapsulation affects component styling and why ::ng-deep should only be used as a temporary workaround rather than a long-term solution.

Engineering Lessons
Today’s session wasn’t just about Angular APIs.
It reinforced a few software engineering principles that are applicable across any technology stack.
One of my favorites was the Rule of Three:

• First time: Write it.

• Second time: Copy it.

• Third time: Refactor it.
Instead of creating reusable helper methods too early, I learned to wait until duplication naturally appears. It keeps the codebase simpler and avoids unnecessary abstractions.
I also learned to prefer semantic CSS classes over generic selectors. A small change like styling .login-button instead of every button element prevents unintended side effects as an application grows.

Looking Ahead
The login page is now complete and responsive, but the real authentication flow starts next.
In the next session, I’ll begin building the AuthService and integrate the login screen with a simulated backend, gradually moving toward a complete enterprise authentication module.
Every day, this project reminds me that rebuilding skills isn’t about memorizing syntax. It’s about understanding the reasoning behind design decisions and writing code that’s maintainable, scalable, and production-ready.
Today’s Key Takeaway
“Good software isn’t built by knowing every API. It’s built by understanding why each design decision is made.”

If you’re also refreshing your Angular knowledge or exploring modern Angular development, I’d love to hear what practices or features have made the biggest difference in your projects. See you in Day 5.
